byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: About 755 million people, three in four of them in villages, and fewer than half of those over the age of seven could read.

items.title: Population
items.summary: India's population was about 755 million in 1984; the census of 1981 had counted about 683 million.

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A newborn in 1984 could expect to live about 56 years.

items.title: Who could read
items.summary: At the 1981 census 36 to 44 percent of people could read and write, 47 to 56 percent of men and 25 to 30 percent of women.

items.title: Town and village
items.summary: About 24 percent of Indians lived in towns and cities.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: Nestlé launched Maggi noodles in India in 1983, as a quick snack for working mothers and children.

items.title: Maggi noodles
items.summary: Nestlé launched Maggi noodles in India in 1983, as a quick snack for working mothers and children.

items.title: Thums Up
items.summary: After Coca-Cola left India in 1977, local colas such as Thums Up and Campa Cola filled the gap.

items.title: Waiting for a gas connection
items.summary: LPG cylinders were rationed and new connections took months or years.

items.title: The Amul girl
items.summary: Amul's butter hoardings, with the cartoon girl, were a fixture in cities.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Terry-cotton and polyester shirts and sarees were widely worn because they were cheap and long-lasting.

items.title: Terry-cotton shirts
items.summary: Terry-cotton and polyester shirts and sarees were widely worn because they were cheap and long-lasting.

items.title: The school uniform
items.summary: School uniforms with ties and badges were standard for children in cities.

items.title: Fashion from films
items.summary: Film stars set the style for hairstyles, sunglasses and tailors' copies of film costumes.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A long textile strike led by Datta Samant began in January 1982 and left tens of thousands of mill workers jobless.

items.title: The Bombay mill strike
items.summary: A long textile strike led by Datta Samant began in January 1982 and left tens of thousands of mill workers jobless.

items.title: Jobs at Maruti
items.summary: Maruti Udyog's factory at Gurgaon began making cars in 1983 with Suzuki's help.

items.title: The secure government job
items.summary: Public sector and government jobs were prized for their security and pension.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: The University Grants Commission began a countrywide classroom telecast on Doordarshan in 1984.

items.title: Lessons on television
items.summary: The University Grants Commission began a countrywide classroom telecast on Doordarshan in 1984.

items.title: Navodaya Vidyalayas
items.summary: The government prepared the Navodaya residential schools for talented rural children, launched in 1985.

items.title: Board exams
items.summary: The class 10 and class 12 board exams decided a child's later options.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: The 'people's car' had a waiting list of almost three years.

items.title: Waiting for a Maruti
items.summary: Buyers booked a Maruti 800 directly with Maruti Udyog and often waited almost three years for delivery, which led to black-market resale premiums of as much as 40 percent; the first car was handed over by Indira Gandhi on 14 December 1983.

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1984 railway or bus fares, or journey times.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: A telephone was something to wait for.

items.title: A waiting list for a line
items.summary: In Bhopal 4,085 people were waiting for a telephone on 31 December 1984, and the Government said the list would be cleared in three years.

sources.label: Lok Sabha: written answer on telephone waiting lists, 23 April 1985

items.title: Universal immunisation
items.summary: India's Universal Immunization Programme started in 1985 to reach all children with vaccines.

items.title: Oral rehydration
items.summary: Oral rehydration salts were promoted to treat diarrhoea in children.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: Video cassette recorders and video parlours let families watch films at home.

items.title: The VCR
items.summary: Video cassette recorders and video parlours let families watch films at home.

items.title: Asia Cup
items.summary: India won the first Asia Cup in Sharjah in 1984.

items.title: P.T. Usha at Los Angeles
items.summary: P.T. Usha finished fourth in the 400 m hurdles at the 1984 Olympics, missing a medal by a hundredth of a second.

items.title: The 1983 World Cup
items.summary: India's win at the 1983 cricket World Cup was still fresh in people's minds and filled playgrounds with young cricketers.

spotlight.title: Television arrives in the living room
spotlight.standfirst: Colour came in 1982, the network split in two in 1984, and in July a family serial gave 50 million viewers an evening ritual.

items.title: Colour in 1982
items.summary: Doordarshan introduced a national channel in 1982, and colour television began with the live telecast of Indira Gandhi's Independence Day speech on 15 August 1982, followed by the colour broadcast of the Asian Games in Delhi.

items.title: Two channels
items.summary: Two years later, in 1984, Doordarshan became a structured network: its sole channel was split into DD-1, broadcast nationally, and DD-2, aimed at the cities.

items.title: A serial for fifty million
items.summary: Hum Log, scripted by Manohar Shyam Joshi, ran on Doordarshan from 7 July 1984 to 17 December 1985, 65 episodes with each viewed by more than 50 million people; it dealt with family planning, dowry, caste harmony and women's empowerment.

items.title: Letters to Ashok Kumar
items.summary: Actor Ashok Kumar closed each episode of Hum Log in conversation with the audience, in Hindi couplets and limericks, and received over 400,000 letters from young viewers asking him to help them persuade their parents to accept their chosen marriage partners.

items.title: A million sets a year
items.summary: A 1984 parliamentary answer estimated television receiver production in 1984 at between 10 lakh and 12 lakh (1 to 1.2 million) sets, colour and black-and-white together, and an industry note says colour television grew by 140.3 percent in 1984-85.

sources.label: Lok Sabha: written answer on television receiver production, 21 March 1984
